strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward, unposed multi-view 3D stylization with 3D Gaussian outputs, which is practically appealing compared with per-scene optimization methods.

The high-level architecture is sensible: separating geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction, and using global cross-attention for style injection, is a plausible design for preserving geometry while transferring appearance.
The proposed voxel-space style loss is well motivated as an extension of 2D style-statistics matching to geometry-aligned multi-view features.
The paper includes useful ablations for style-content coupling and style-loss variants, and reports both short-range and long-range consistency metrics.
Qualitative results suggest that the method can produce attractive stylized renderings across several scenes and styles.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to VGGT/AnySplat-style feed-forward 3D reconstruction plus standard AdaIN/VGG statistics losses; the paper does not clearly isolate how much improvement comes from the new stylization components versus the strong pretrained reconstruction backbone.

The experimental comparison is limited. The most directly relevant concurrent feed-forward stylization method, Styl3R, is not compared, and the paper only compares against StyleRF and StyleGS on a small set of Tanks and Temples scenes.

The evaluation metrics do not fully support the main claims. LPIPS/RMSE between nearby stylized views measure temporal/view consistency but not necessarily style fidelity or geometric correctness; ArtScore is reference-free and may not measure whether the target style was faithfully transferred.
The ablation gains for the 3D style loss are modest numerically, especially for short-range LPIPS, making the central loss contribution less convincing than the qualitative discussion suggests.

Important implementation details are missing or underspecified, including loss weights, training resolution, number of views used in training, voxel grid construction, feature aggregation details, optimizer settings, and compute cost.

There is an apparent inconsistency between the 3D style loss description, which claims fused multi-view voxel statistics, and Algorithm 3, which appears to voxelize and compute statistics per view inside the view loop.

The comparison to per-scene baselines may be difficult to interpret: the proposed method is trained on DL3DV and tested zero-shot, while baselines use released per-scene weights, but runtime, training cost, and input-view conditions are not comprehensively normalized or analyzed.
Reproducibility is limited because the code is only promised upon acceptance, and the appendix pseudo-code is not sufficient to reproduce the method.

The paper makes broad claims about scaling to hundreds of views, but the experiments show quality degradation beyond 32 views and training uses no more than 24 views, so the scalability claim is only partially supported.

strengths: The problem is timely and relevant: feed-forward, pose-free multi-view 3D stylization with Gaussian splatting would be valuable if convincingly demonstrated.
The paper presents a coherent architecture that separates geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction, building on strong recent feed-forward 3D reconstruction components.
The voxel-space style loss is a reasonable idea for encouraging multi-view consistency, and the paper includes some ablations over attention strategy and style-loss variants.
Qualitative results are visually plausible in several examples, and the method appears faster/more general than per-scene stylization methods in spirit.
weaknesses: The contribution appears highly incremental: much of the system is inherited from VGGT/AnySplat-style feed-forward reconstruction, while the style branch resembles standard cross-attention conditioning plus AdaIN/VGG statistics. The paper does not clearly isolate what is technically novel beyond this combination.

The evaluation is too narrow for a top-tier acceptance. Main comparisons use only StyleRF and StyleGS on four Tanks and Temples scenes, with no comparison to the most relevant concurrent/nearby feed-forward method Styl3R, and no broader set of scenes, styles, or categories.

The comparison setup is not fully convincing. The baselines are evaluated using released per-scene weights while Stylos is a separately trained feed-forward model; it is unclear whether the inputs, style references, rendering resolutions, and evaluation protocols are matched fairly.

The quantitative metrics do not adequately support the central claims. LPIPS/RMSE between short- and long-range stylized frames are weak proxies for cross-view 3D consistency unless geometry/visibility alignment is carefully defined, and ArtScore is reference-free and not sufficient evidence of faithful style transfer.

Ablations are shallow. There is no convincing decomposition of the full training objective, including the roles of CLIP loss, content loss, TV regularization, reconstruction loss during stage 2, VGG layers, voxel resolution, confidence weighting, number of views, or frozen-vs-trainable components.

The claimed 3D style loss is underspecified and somewhat inconsistent with the pseudo-code: the text describes multi-view voxel fusion, but Algorithm 3 appears to voxelize and match statistics inside a per-view loop, which weakens confidence in the formulation.

The paper makes strong claims about scaling to hundreds of views, but the evidence shows quality degradation beyond 32 views and training uses no more than 24 views. This undercuts the scalability claim.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper promises code release only upon acceptance and omits many implementation details such as training schedules, hyperparameters, voxel grid settings, style sampling, losses weights, model size, compute budget, and exact splits.
The experimental section lacks human preference studies or style-faithfulness evaluation, which are especially important for stylization papers where perceptual quality is central.

Writing and presentation contain several rough edges, including placeholder code-release text, duplicated references, typos, and overclaiming relative to the evidence. Overall, the work is plausible but not yet competitive for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward, reference-guided 3D stylization from unposed single- or multi-view inputs, which is practically valuable for 3D content creation.

The proposed system is technically coherent, combining a strong geometry backbone with a style-conditioning pathway and explicit Gaussian output; the separation of geometry and style prediction is intuitive and well motivated.
The voxel-based 3D style loss is a meaningful contribution beyond standard 2D style statistics, and the ablation suggests it improves cross-view consistency, especially long-range RMSE/LPIPS.
The paper includes comparisons to representative 3D stylization baselines and shows encouraging zero-shot performance despite using a single trained model rather than per-scene optimization.
Qualitative results are visually compelling, and the method appears to preserve geometry while transferring style more consistently than the shown baselines.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental because the method relies heavily on VGGT/AnySplat-style feed-forward reconstruction, standard cross-attention, AdaIN-style statistics, VGG losses, and CLIP/TV regularization; the main new pieces are useful but not radically new.

The evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest: held-out CO3D categories and only four Tanks and Temples scenes may not fully support broad claims of generalization to arbitrary scenes, categories, and styles.

The strongest contemporary baseline, Styl3R, is not compared because code is unavailable. This is understandable, but it weakens positioning given that it targets a very similar instant 3D stylization setting.

Several reported gains are modest, especially for the 3D style loss ablation, where improvements over image/scene losses are small and not accompanied by statistical analysis or broader category/style coverage.
Style quality evaluation relies heavily on ArtScore and qualitative figures; there is no user study or stronger perceptual evaluation, and reference-style faithfulness is not deeply quantified.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is promised only upon acceptance, and key training details such as hyperparameters, compute, dataset sampling, exact loss weights, and implementation details of voxelization/style fusion are not fully specified.
The claim of scaling from single view to hundreds of views is only partially supported; the paper itself reports visual degradation beyond 32 views and training with no more than 24 views.

The comparison setup is not fully disentangled: Stylos is trained on large-scale DL3DV, while baselines use released per-scene weights, making it hard to isolate architectural advantages from data/training differences.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward, pose-free multi-view 3D stylization with 3D Gaussian outputs and a single style reference.

The architecture is sensible: separating geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction is a clean design choice, and global content-style attention is well motivated for multi-view consistency.
The proposed voxel-space style loss is a plausible extension of AdaIN/statistics-based style losses to 3D, and the paper provides ablations comparing image-, scene-, and voxel-level variants.
Experiments include several relevant baselines, both per-scene optimization methods and the closest feed-forward method Styl3R, with consistency, style-quality, and efficiency metrics.
The qualitative results are generally compelling, and the paper includes useful failure cases, implementation details, and supplemental results.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence for the central 3D style loss is weaker than claimed: quantitative gains over the scene-level loss are very small in Table 2, with ArtScore essentially tied and consistency differences marginal.

Evaluation scope is limited for strong generalization claims. Main state-of-the-art comparisons are on only four Tanks & Temples scenes, and some ablations use only three CO3D categories or 15 held-out scenes.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing. Baselines and Stylos are evaluated at different resolutions/settings, rendering cost is excluded from some timing analysis, and failed StylizedGS cases are excluded from some reported metrics, which may bias conclusions.

Several metrics are imperfect proxies for the desired behavior. LPIPS/RMSE consistency can reward under-stylized or over-smoothed outputs, while ArtScore/ArtFID do not directly measure fidelity to the given reference style or preservation of 3D geometry.

Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines VGGT/AnySplat-style feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction, transformer cross-attention for style conditioning, and AdaIN-like statistics in voxel space. The contribution is useful but not clearly transformative.

Important technical details are under-specified, including the exact CLIP loss, VGG layer weights, style/content training sampling, and some details of voxelized feature aggregation, making independent reproduction difficult before code release.
The paper claims scalability to hundreds of views, but training uses at most around 20-24 views and the authors observe degradation beyond 32 views, so the scalability claim is overstated.

The method inherits substantial limitations from the geometry backbone, and failure cases show that reconstruction errors, high-frequency structures, and extreme styles can significantly degrade results.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely problem: feed-forward 3D stylization from unposed single- or multi-view inputs, which would be useful if demonstrated convincingly.

The proposed system is clearly motivated and combines sensible components: a VGGT/AnySplat-like geometry backbone, a style-conditioned color pathway, global cross-attention, and a voxel-space style-statistics loss.
The paper includes several relevant baselines, ablations over attention topology and style loss design, and qualitative examples/failure cases in the appendix.
The claimed efficiency advantage over per-scene optimization methods is practically meaningful, and the single-forward framing is a reasonable direction for 3D content creation.
weaknesses: The novelty appears limited. Much of the method is a composition of VGGT/AnySplat-style feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction, standard cross-attention style conditioning, AdaIN/VGG statistics, CLIP loss, and voxel aggregation. The paper does not sufficiently isolate what is technically new beyond this integration.

The evaluation is not convincing enough for the central claims. The strongest claim is geometry-aware, view-consistent 3D stylization, but the main quantitative evidence relies on LPIPS/RMSE consistency and ArtScore/ArtFID, which are indirect and can favor smooth or under-stylized outputs. There is no user study or stronger perceptual evaluation despite the subjective nature of style quality.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns. Single-forward methods are evaluated at preset lower resolutions while 3DGS optimization methods use full resolution; per-scene optimization time is counted for some methods but training time is excluded for feed-forward models; and StylizedGS is omitted from the main quantitative table due to failures, with failure cases excluded elsewhere for 'fair' comparison. These choices make the reported superiority hard to trust.

The closest feed-forward baseline, Styl3R, is only partially compared, with missing entries in key tables and limited discussion of why it fails or whether the setup matches its intended operating regime. This weakens the positioning against the most relevant prior work.

The ablations are narrow and sometimes weakly supported. The attention ablation is mostly reconstruction-focused rather than stylization-focused, and the 3D style loss improves consistency metrics only marginally over image/scene losses while the paper makes strong qualitative claims from a small number of examples.

Scalability claims are overstated. The method is advertised as scaling to hundreds of views, but training samples at most around 20-24 views, quality degrades beyond 32 views, and the efficiency analysis reports only up to 64 views and excludes rendering cost.

Technical details are insufficient for full reproducibility. The code is promised only upon acceptance, many implementation choices for voxelization, feature fusion, losses, style dataset composition, and evaluation protocols are under-specified, and the empty code URL in the abstract is concerning.

The method depends heavily on VGGT reconstruction quality, and the limitations show that reconstruction failures directly cause stylization failures. This dependency undermines the broader generalization claims, especially for high-frequency geometry, clutter, large view counts, and strong color/lighting styles.

Writing and presentation contain numerous issues, including typos, grammar problems, unclear equations, and inconsistent terminology. These do not by themselves determine the score, but they contribute to a lack of polish and make some experimental details harder to verify.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward, unposed multi-view 3D stylization with view consistency and no per-scene optimization. This is a practically meaningful setting where prior NeRF/3DGS stylization methods are often too slow or scene-specific.

The architecture is sensible and well motivated, separating geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction, and the global cross-attention design is supported by ablations showing better reconstruction than frame-only or hybrid coupling.

The voxel-space 3D style loss is a useful contribution: it extends image/scene-level style statistics into a geometry-aware fused representation, and qualitative examples suggest improved cross-view coherence and texture placement.

The paper compares against several recent 3D stylization baselines, including StyleGaussian, G-Style, SGSST, StylizedGS, and the closely related Styl3R, and reports both consistency and stylization-quality metrics.

The efficiency advantage is compelling: a single-forward model with reported 0.05s stylization time is a clear practical benefit over per-scene optimization methods, and the paper includes a scaling analysis over view counts.
The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful architecture diagrams, ablations, failure cases, and many qualitative examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental because the method relies heavily on VGGT/AnySplat-style feed-forward 3D reconstruction and standard style-transfer losses; the main new pieces are the style-conditioning pathway and voxelized style loss rather than a fundamentally new 3D stylization formulation.

The empirical evidence for the 3D style loss over a simpler scene-level loss is not very strong quantitatively: in Table 2, improvements are small for consistency metrics and ArtScore is nearly identical to the scene-level loss, so the central loss contribution rests heavily on qualitative examples.

The evaluation scope is narrower than the claims suggest. Main quantitative comparison uses only four Tanks & Temples scenes, and the CO3D ablation uses 15 held-out scenes. This is limited for claims about broad generalization to unseen categories, scenes, styles, and hundreds of views.

Some comparisons may favor the proposed method or are not fully clean. StylizedGS is excluded from main quantitative tables due to failures, Styl3R has missing results for one scene, and feed-forward methods are evaluated at different preset resolutions. The timing comparison includes training time for optimization baselines but not model training/amortization for Stylos, which is reasonable for deployment but should be framed carefully.

The closest related method, Styl3R, deserves deeper comparison. The paper says Styl3R is mainly designed for 2-8 views and less focused on consistency, but the experimental analysis does not fully isolate this distinction across matched input counts, resolutions, and output settings.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the code link appears blank in the abstract, implementation release is promised upon acceptance, and several important details of voxelization, confidence weighting, feature fusion, and training data composition are only partially specified.

The claim that the method scales from a single view to hundreds of views is overstated. The paper itself reports quality degradation beyond 32 views and training uses no more than about 20-24 views, so the strongest demonstrated operating regime is more modest.

The evaluation lacks human preference studies or task-specific perceptual assessment, which is important for artistic stylization where automated metrics such as ArtScore, ArtFID, LPIPS, and RMSE may not fully capture style fidelity, aesthetics, or temporal/view consistency.

Ablations are incomplete for the full training objective: the contributions of CLIP loss, TV regularization, content loss, DINO/style-token design, and freezing strategy are not separately studied, making it hard to attribute the final performance gains precisely.
The presentation has some polish issues, including typos, missing code URL, and occasional imprecise language, though these do not substantially impair understanding.
